Williamson County by the numbers

Who keeps property records in Williamson County, Texas?

The Williamson County Clerk keeps them. Deeds, liens, releases of liens, plats, restrictions, trusts and similar instruments go into the Official Public Records the clerk maintains.

The same office also runs the probate court clerk's work, the commissioners court clerk's work and local birth, marriage and death registration. For a seller, the part that matters is land recording, because every deed, deed of trust release and lien notice that touches a Williamson County house lands there.

  • Land recording and vital records counter: 1848 Texas Trail, Georgetown, TX 78626.
  • Court filings: the Justice Center, 405 Martin Luther King St., Georgetown.
  • Phone: 512-943-1515. Mailing address: PO Box 647, Jarrell, TX 76537-0647.
  • The recording counter opens at 8 a.m. and shuts at 4:30 each weekday afternoon; the court floor stays open an extra half hour.

The county clerk page says staff do not perform searches for the public, citing Attorney General Opinion WW-607, and cannot give legal advice. Plan on running your own search or asking a title company to do it.

How do I search Williamson County property records?

Use the clerk's Search Records page, which links to an Official Public Records Search, a judicial records search and a link for military discharge records.

Start with the owner name from your deed or tax bill, then look for anything recorded after it: a deed of trust, a release of lien, an abstract of judgment, a notice of foreclosure sale or an affidavit. A release that was never recorded is the most common reason a lien still shows against a house the owner thinks is paid off. If you find one, the lender has to record a release in the same office, because Local Government Code 192.007, as quoted on the clerk's site, requires any action on a recorded instrument to be made by recording another instrument in the same manner.

The county site also carries a map viewer, and ownership and value sit with the Williamson Central Appraisal District. Ownership on the appraisal roll can lag the deed records, so treat the clerk's records as the source for who holds title.

What must a deed have to be accepted in Georgetown?

A deed needs the owner's signature plus either an acknowledgment by a notary or other authorized officer or an oath before two witnesses. The Texas Courts clerk manual cites Property Code 12.001(b) for this.

A house here is recorded in Georgetown, even if the owner lives in another state. The county fee page also asks filers to bring a current photo ID with the document and payment, citing House Bill 1195 of the 88th Legislature.

Deed records the manual lists include general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds, plus affidavits, releases of deeds of trust, leases, contracts of sale and powers of attorney. Recording does not make a defective deed valid. It gives public notice of what the paper says.

What does recording a document cost?

The clerk's current schedule is the Williamson County 2024 Recording Fees PDF on the Fees page. The state manual below is the statutory base, so ask the clerk for the county total first.

Texas county clerk recording fee structure (2023 County Clerk Manual, Texas Courts)
ChargeAmount printed in the manual
First page$5.00
Each added page, part page or attachment$4.00
Each name over five indexed$0.25
Records management and preservationNot more than $10
Records archiveNot more than $10
Records technology and infrastructure$2.00

A deed with no grantee mailing address can draw an added charge of $25, per the same manual. A commissioners court may direct the clerk to waive real property recording fees for buyers using certain grant programs, so ask the clerk whether Williamson County has done so.

How can an owner guard against a fraudulent deed or lien?

Property Fraud Alert is a free notification service listed on the clerk's page. It emails or phones you each time a new document is filed under a name you choose.

If a judgment lien or conveyance looks fraudulent, the county's page lays out four steps through the District Clerk.

  • Petition the District Clerk.
  • File an Owner's Affidavit of Purported Conveyance.
  • Wait while a district judge reviews and signs findings of fact and conclusions of law.
  • Record a certified copy of the signed order in the Official Public Records, which the page says is free.

The page cites Government Code 51.902 and 51.903 for this process and suggests asking the District Clerk about a temporary restraining order. Get legal advice before filing.

Where do foreclosure notices and sales happen in Williamson County?

The county's trustee sale page puts the auctions on the month's first Tuesday, outside the Justice Center at 405 MLK Street in Georgetown.

Texas State Law Library guidance says the lender's notice of sale must go out three weeks or more ahead, hang on the courthouse door and be filed with the clerk. A borrower who gets a notice of default may reinstate by paying the past due amount within 20 days of receiving it.

If a notice is recorded against your house, the clerk's records will show it. A sale before the auction date is possible, with the lender paid from the buyer's funds. Request the payoff in writing from the servicer.

How do I record transfers after a death in Williamson County?

The paper to record depends on how the owner's estate is handled, and the State Law Library lists the pairings.

  • Transfer on death deed: affidavit of death and death certificate.
  • Administered estate: executor's or administrator's deed.
  • Muniment of title: court order plus the will.
  • No court route: affidavit of heirship, a sworn statement a buyer is not legally forced to accept.

The probate side of the clerk's office takes applications and small estate affidavits, which under Estates Code chapter 205 cover estates with no will and no more than $75,000 in assets outside homestead and exempt property, and need court approval.

The county cannot add heirs to an old deed. Whoever takes title records the proving paper, then the sale deed follows.

How big and how fast growing is Williamson County?

Census estimates put Williamson County at 752,827 people in July 2025, a 23.6 percent jump over the April 2020 base, spread across roughly 1,116 square miles of land.

Homeownership sits at 66.4 percent of housing units, and QuickFacts lists $447,000 as the middle value for 2020 to 2024. The median gross rent runs $1,796 a month. The county issued 4,956 building permits in 2025, which tells you new construction competes with resale listings.

Fast growth means many houses changed hands recently and sit under recent deeds and loans, which makes the record search quick. Older rural parcels, inherited homes and houses with unreleased liens are the ones that need paper cleanup before closing.

More questions about Williamson County, TX Property Records

Does the Williamson County Clerk run searches for me?

No. The clerk's page says the office does not perform searches for the public, citing Attorney General Opinion WW-607. Use the online Official Public Records Search or ask a title company.

Is photo ID required at the Williamson County recording counter?

Yes. The county Fees page requires a current photo ID along with the document and payment, and cites House Bill 1195.

Where can I find the exact recording fee?

On the clerk's Fees page, which links the 2024 Recording Fees PDF. The state manual figures in the table above are only the statutory base.

Can I sell my Williamson County house with a lien on it?

Often yes, because a lien can be paid off when the sale closes. A title company can find the recorded lien, request the payoff and arrange the release, including when the lender never recorded one.

Is the county clerk the same office as the tax office?

No. The county tax assessor-collector and the Williamson Central Appraisal District are separate offices. The clerk records documents and keeps probate and commissioners court records.

Harris County by the numbers

Where do you record a deed or lien release in Harris County?

The Harris County Clerk's Real Property Department records documents tied to real estate, and it will accept anything a statute authorizes, requires and permits to be filed. In person, go to 201 Caroline, 3rd Floor, Suite 320, Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The department's phone number is (713) 274-8680.

Plan to arrive early. Everyone entering the building passes through security, the door to Suite 320 locks promptly at 4:30 p.m., and you must be inside before 4:00 p.m. to get a non-certified copy. Because Harris County has more than 3.3 million residents, the clerk may require a photo ID from a person filing in person, and the clerk's page says each filer must show their own government-issued identification.

Releases of lien can also go to the annex offices, but the clerk warns that those can take five to seven business days to reach the downtown office. For a closing on a deadline, file downtown or use e-recording.

Can you mail or e-record a document to the Harris County Clerk?

Yes to both, with limits. Mailed originals go to the clerk's Attn: Real Property Department at P.O. Box 1525, Houston, TX 77251-1525, and the postal service delivers only to that box. Couriers with a tracking number use 201 Caroline, 4th Floor, Suite 460 on weekdays.

Mail payment must be a cashier's check, a money order or an approved business or firm check drawn on a U.S. bank. The clerk does not take cash or personal checks by mail, and it rejects temporary, estate, trust or association checks and any check with mark-outs.

E-recording must run through an approved provider. The clerk's page names Corporation Service Company, eRecording Partners Network and Simplifile as examples. Texas law limits who may e-file to groups such as licensed attorneys, banks and credit unions, title insurance companies and agents, state agencies and municipal clerks. A document queued before 2:00 p.m. central time is processed the same business day, and anything later waits until the next one.

What does Harris County charge to record real property?

The clerk's real property fee schedule lists a handful of base charges, shown below as printed. A deed with a few pages and no more than five names to index sits at the low end of the range.

Harris County Clerk real property fee schedule
ChargeAmountSource

Each additional page$4.00Same page
Each name over five indexed$0.25Same page

The office raised its records management and archive fees from $6.00 to $10.00. A condominium declaration is recorded at $10.00 per taped sheet, and each key map page attached to a condo filing is $50.

What does the Harris County Clerk require on a document before accepting it?

The clerk accepts only original documents or certified copies of court documents, and a photocopy will not be recorded. A rejected filing costs time, so check the list before you send anything.

  • The signer's signature must be an original and must be notarized, except for an IRS release.
  • Names are printed under every signature, with the capacity of the signer and the entity named.
  • The document needs legal descriptions where they apply and a printed return address.
  • Leave a margin of 1 to 2 inches across the top and left side for recording information.
  • A conveyance must show each grantee's address, or the filer pays the greater of $25 or twice the recording fee.
  • An abstract of judgment must show the plaintiff's mailing address.

An original will cannot be filed in the real property records. A will goes to the Probate Department for safekeeping, and a probated will can be recorded as a certified copy issued by the probate court. A will can also be attached as an exhibit to an affidavit of heirship.

How do you get copies of Harris County property records and guard against fraud?

The clerk's eCommerce feature lets the public buy certified and non-certified copies of recorded documents, and the Public Records Department at 713-274-6390 answers questions about it.

The clerk also offers the free Property Alert System, which notifies homeowners when a new real property document is filed under their name. Owners who rent out a house, who have heirs, or who have a title question should sign up before listing, since an unexpected filing is easier to fix before a buyer finds it.

Value and ownership for tax purposes come from the Harris Central Appraisal District at hcad.org. A title company reads these records for liens, judgments and unresolved heirs, and a sale usually pauses until each item is released or paid.

Which recorded documents decide how fast a Harris County sale can close?

A title company reads the chain of recorded papers, and each type has its own home in the clerk's files. Gaps are most common after a death or a missed mortgage payment.

  • After an owner dies, the route depends on the estate: an executor's or administrator's deed for an administered estate, a court order plus the will for a muniment of title, or an affidavit of heirship when neither applies.
  • A transfer on death deed only works if it was recorded before the owner died, and the recorded affidavit of death and the death certificate follow it.
  • A foreclosure sale notice must be filed with the clerk and posted at the courthouse at least 21 days before the first-Tuesday auction, which the state sets between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.
  • A deed of trust is cleared by a recorded release of lien, which the clerk accepts downtown and at annexes.

The Texas State Law Library notes that a county cannot rewrite an old deed to add heirs, so the fix is a new recorded instrument. Start the paperwork before listing the house, because an affidavit or court order can take longer to arrange than the sale itself.

How large is the Harris County housing market?

Harris County is the most populous county in Texas: the July 2025 estimate is 5,045,026 people, up from 4,731,145 at the 2020 census. It spans 1,706.96 square miles of land and counted 2,012,848 housing units, and 30,909 building permits were issued in 2025.

Owners live in 54.7 percent of homes, and renters have the rest. For 2020 to 2024 the Census Bureau lists a median home value of $276,600, a median rent of $1,401 and a median household income of $74,983. People 65 and older are 13.1 percent of residents, 26.8 percent were born abroad, and 151,833 are veterans.

A county this large produces a large volume of recorded documents, from deeds of trust to liens to affidavits of heirship. That volume is one reason the clerk insists on clean originals, precise fees and approved e-recording vendors.

More questions about Harris County, TX Property Records

Where is the Harris County Clerk's real property office?

The in-person counter is at 201 Caroline, 3rd Floor, Suite 320, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The Real Property Department's phone number is (713) 274-8680.

Does the Harris County Clerk require a photo ID to file?

Yes, for in-person filing. Texas law lets a clerk in a county of 3.3 million or more require photo identification, and the clerk's page says each person must present their own valid government-issued ID.

Can I record a copy of my deed in Harris County?

No. The clerk accepts original documents with original signatures, or certified copies of court documents. Photocopies of a deed will be refused.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Harris County?

The posted schedule is $5.00 for the first page, $4.00 for each added page, $0.25 for each name over five, plus a $10.00 archive fee and a $10.00 management fee. Check the clerk's page for the latest amounts.

How do I get alerts when someone files a document under my name?

Sign up for the Harris County Clerk's free Property Alert System. It notifies homeowners of any new real property document filed under their name.

Dallas County by the numbers

Where are Dallas County property records kept?

Deeds, mortgages, releases and other land records for Dallas County sit with the County Clerk's Recording Division in the Records Building at 500 Elm Street, Suite 2100, Dallas, TX 75202. The division describes itself as the recorder of deeds and keeper of the Official Public Records.

By the clerk's own count the office records roughly 400,000 documents a year. That stream includes deeds, liens against a property, transfers between owners, probate papers that touch land, and the release of lien filed once a mortgage is paid off. The stated purpose is to tell the public who holds a financial interest in a parcel.

  • Phone: (214) 653-7099
  • Hours: opens 8:00 a.m., closes 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, with court-approved holidays excepted
  • Mail: Dallas County Clerk's Office, Recording Division, 500 Elm Street, STE 2100, Dallas, Texas 75202
  • Questions the FAQ page does not answer: recording@dallascounty.org

Anyone selling a house in Dallas County will touch this office through the title company, since the title search and the filing of the new deed both run through these records. The clerk's Recording Division page is the place to start.

How do I search and copy Dallas County records?

Start with the clerk's Online Public Record Search, which returns non-certified images, then buy a certified copy only if a lender, court or title company asks for one. The clerk states plainly that the free search and the certified service are two different things.

Certified electronic copies of Official Public Record documents are sold on the clerk's website around the clock. Each one carries the clerk's digital signature and tamper-proof encryption, so a buyer's lender can accept it without a paper original. In person or by mail, the clerk prices real property copies at $1.00 per page for a plain copy, and $1.00 per page plus a $5.00 certification fee per document for a certified one.

Plat copies are priced separately: $6.00 per page for the large 18 by 24 size and $1.00 per page for 8.5 by 11, with the same $5.00 per-plat certification fee on certified copies. The clerk keeps only the plats filed with that office, so a subdivision map recorded elsewhere will not be there.

Recorded deeds sometimes carry a Social Security number, driver's license number, date of birth or bank account number. Under House Bill 2061, the clerk says that kind of information may be eligible for redaction. The owner files a Redaction Request Form by mail or in person. Once a document is recorded, any other change needs a later filing, and the clerk suggests asking a lawyer whether a correction document or a fresh deed is the right fix.

What are the Dallas County Clerk's recording charges?

The first page of a standard document costs $25.00 and every page after it costs $4.00. The clerk breaks the first-page charge into $5.00 for recording, $10.00 for records preservation and $10.00 for archiving.

Selected Dallas County Clerk recording and copy fees, from the clerk's fee page
ItemFee as printed

Each remaining page$4.00 per page

Federal tax lien, real estate or personal property$30.00

Certification added to a copy$5.00 per document

Any writing on the back of the last sheet is billed as a full $4.00 page, so a signature block that spills onto a reverse side costs the same as a new page. The clerk also lists specialty documents with their own fees, and a few filings, such as child support liens and military discharge papers, carry no filing fee.

Payment rules are strict. The office takes cash, money orders, cashier's checks and business checks made out to the Dallas County Clerk, and it does not accept personal checks. Cards work only in person, with a 2.05 percent convenience fee on credit and pinless debit or $2.85 on pin debit. The fee page adds that filings sent by mail need a self-addressed stamped envelope for the file-stamped copy.

What does the Dallas County Clerk require before recording a deed?

The deed has to be signed and properly acknowledged, and for deeds conveying property between people the clerk now asks for a photo ID. Under House Bill 1195, photo ID has been required since July 1, 2023 on documents that convey property from one person to another.

  • Acknowledgment. A deed can be recorded only if it is acknowledged or sworn before an authorized officer such as a notary, or witnessed by two subscribing witnesses, according to the Texas county clerk manual.
  • Court-ordered papers. A document that comes from a court action must be a certified copy authenticated by the court or its clerk.
  • Grantee address. The manual notes that a missing grantee mailing address can add a $25 charge.
  • Notary on site. The FAQ says a notary sits on the fourth floor in the Treasurer's office from 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. daily for $10, cash only.
  • Electronic filing. Local Government Code Sec. 195.003 limits e-recording to attorneys, banks and credit unions, federally approved lenders, licensed regulated lenders, licensed title insurers and agents, and state agencies.

That last point matters for owners selling without an agent. An individual who is not on the list files on paper at the Elm Street counter or by mail, or lets the title company submit the deed electronically after closing.

What do Dallas County's numbers mean for a seller?

Dallas County has a lower owner-occupied rate than Denton County (65.5 percent) or Ellis County (75.8 percent), and that shapes the mix of sales. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page puts the owner-occupied rate at 50.8 percent for 2020 to 2024, so roughly half of households rent. A seller whose house is leased out should expect a buyer or title company to ask for the lease and tenant details.

The same page lists a July 2025 population estimate of 2,661,397, up 1.9 percent from the 2020 base, spread over 873.06 square miles of land and 1,099,775 housing units. The 2020 count was 2,613,539 people, or 2,993.6 per square mile. The typical owner-occupied house is valued at $303,000, median gross rent is $1,565, and median household income is $76,547 in 2024 dollars. Builders pulled 12,691 permits in 2025.

Median monthly owner costs run $2,166 with a mortgage and $793 without one. That gap shows up at a closing table: a house with no mortgage is simpler to transfer because there is no lender payoff and no release of lien to track down.

Which record problems slow a Dallas County sale?

Unreleased liens, unfiled estate paperwork and tax debts cause most of the delays, and all of them show up in the records the clerk keeps. A title company runs the search before closing and flags what it finds.

  • Old mortgages. A paid-off loan should have a recorded release of lien. If none was filed, the lender has to be contacted to issue one.
  • Tax liens. State and federal tax lien notices are filed with the clerk, and the clerk lists fixed fees for both and for their releases.
  • Foreclosure notices. A notice of sale is posted at the courthouse and filed with the clerk, usually at least 21 days before the sale, according to the Texas State Law Library.
  • Estates without a clean chain. An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement filed with the clerk, and the State Law Library says no law forces a third party to accept it. A court order or probate may be needed instead.
  • Hospital and child support liens. Both appear on the clerk's fee page and have to be cleared if they attach to the property.

If any of these turn up, ask the title company which instrument cures the problem and who files it.

How do property taxes affect closing on a Dallas County house?

Property tax is a lien on the land from January 1 of each year, and the Comptroller says the person who owned the property that day is liable for that year's bill. A sale in November does not erase the lien; it just shifts who pays it at closing.

Texas bills usually go out around October 1, and taxes unpaid on February 1 become delinquent. The Comptroller prints a six percent penalty and one percent interest on that day, with the penalty growing by one percent each month until July 1. People over 65 or disabled can pay in installments. Ask the Dallas County tax office for the current balance, and ask the county appraisal district whether a homestead exemption is on file, since a buyer who takes the house after January 1 may be able to claim one for the rest of that year if the seller did not.

More questions about Dallas County, TX Property Records

What is the first-page charge for a deed at the Dallas County Clerk?

The first page costs $25.00 and each additional page costs $4.00. The first-page fee is built from $5.00 for recording, $10.00 for records preservation and $10.00 for archiving. Information on the back of a page is charged as a full page.

Can I pay Dallas County recording fees with a personal check?

No. The clerk accepts cash, money orders, cashier's checks and business checks payable to the Dallas County Clerk. Cards are taken only in person, with a 2.05 percent convenience fee on credit and pinless debit cards or $2.85 on pin debit.

Are the documents in the online public record search certified?

No. The clerk says online search results are non-certified. A separate service sells electronic certified copies with the clerk's digital signature, and paper certified copies cost $1.00 per page plus $5.00 per document.

Can I e-record my own deed in Dallas County?

Usually not. Local Government Code Sec. 195.003 limits electronic recording to attorneys, banks, certain lenders, title companies and state agencies. An individual owner normally files on paper at 500 Elm Street or has a title company file the deed.

How do I remove a Social Security number from a recorded Dallas County document?

Submit a Redaction Request Form to the County Clerk's Office by mail or in person. The clerk says House Bill 2061 makes certain personal data, including Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, dates of birth and account numbers, eligible for redaction.

Bexar County by the numbers

Which Bexar County office records deeds and liens?

The Bexar County Clerk's Recordings Division files and maintains real property records, personal property records, notices of trustee sale and public notices. Filing in person happens at the Paul Elizondo Tower, 101 W. Nueva, Suite 103, San Antonio 78205, phone 210-335-2581. A Southside Annex inside Precinct 1 at 3505 Pleasanton Rd. also takes filings, at 210-335-3522.

The doors are open weekdays from 8 a.m., closing at 5 p.m. except Wednesdays, when the office stays open until 5:45. Deed Records, the desk that pulls copies and researches liens, is in Suite B109 of the same tower at 210-335-2273. Mail goes to the Clerk's Office, Attn: Recordings, 100 Dolorosa, Suite 104, San Antonio.

The clerk's site lists a "Records on the Run" satellite office that rotates through precinct offices and community centers each month, so a filer can skip the downtown trip. The clerk also runs a Vanguard Property Alert that warns owners about potentially fraudulent filings, and accepts wills for safekeeping.

What are Bexar County's fees for filing a deed?

Filing a one-page instrument with the Bexar County Clerk costs $25.00, and every added page is $4.00. The first-page charge breaks into a $5.00 recording fee, a $10.00 records archive fee and a $10.00 records management fee, all effective January 1, 2024.

What are the filing rules for Bexar County recordings?

The clerk records only originals with original signatures and will not record a copy. Documents are cashiered, given an instrument number and scanned on the spot, then the originals are handed back or returned. Payment can be cash, credit card, check or money order, with checks written to the Bexar County Clerk.

Electronic filing is a separate lane. Section 195.003 of the Local Government Code limits it to attorneys, banks and credit unions, federally backed mortgage lenders, persons approved to make regulated loans, title companies, state agencies and municipal clerks. The clerk lists six approved e-filing providers, among them CSC, Simplifile, ePN, Indecomm and Hopdox.

The clerk's staff do not draft deeds and do not vouch for a clear title, and they send people who want assurance to title companies and attorneys. A conveyance also has to be signed and acknowledged before a notary or similar officer before it can go on record, a rule the Texas county clerk manual ties to Property Code 12.001(b).

How can a seller check for liens on a Bexar County house?

Start with the clerk's public records search, or visit the Deed Records Department in Suite B109 of the Paul Elizondo Tower, where staff can point you to recorded liens against a property. The clerk does not guarantee clear title and takes no responsibility for encumbrances, so a guaranteed search comes from a title company, with an attorney as the other route.

Mortgage foreclosure notices can be pulled from the same search. A list is also available through the clerk's GIS Foreclosure Map or at the Deed Records counter, while the list of tax foreclosures comes from the law firm that handles them at 210-225-4422.

  • Release of lien: record the original in person at the tower or mail it to the courthouse office, at $25.00 for the first page
  • Lost deed: a certified copy runs $1.00 per page plus $5.00 per certification
  • Plain copies: found online under Land Records in the Official Public Records Search

How do foreclosure sales work in Bexar County?

Mortgage and tax foreclosure sales in Bexar County are public cash auctions held the first Tuesday of each month between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. When that Tuesday falls on January 1 or July 4, the sale moves to Wednesday. Per the clerk, bidding happens outdoors beside the courthouse, in the gap between it and the Paul Elizondo Tower, unless Commissioners Court names a different spot.

Bidders need no registration for a mortgage foreclosure, but registration is required to bid on a tax foreclosure. Only cash or certified funds work, and personal checks are refused. A GIS Foreclosure Map tracks notices and is refreshed twice a month, on the first Friday after the auction and about 18 days before the next sale.

Redemption periods are stated on the clerk's page: two years for agricultural or homestead property and six months for other property, counted from the day the sale deed goes on record. The clerk also hosts a free foreclosure training seminar on the first Tuesday of each month. The State Law Library adds that a notice of sale must be posted and placed on file with the clerk 21 or more days ahead.

How big is Bexar County, and what does its housing look like?

Bexar County spans 1,248 square miles around San Antonio, which serves as both seat and biggest city. The Handbook of Texas places it along the Balcones Escarpment, with hilly Edwards Plateau country in the northwest and flatter prairie and South Texas plains elsewhere. The San Antonio River and the Medina River drain it, and Interstates 10, 35, 37 and 410 plus U.S. 281 and U.S. 90 carry traffic through.

Bexar was established as a county on December 20, 1836. The mission-era area around the Alamo and the five Spanish missions is part of the historic record behind many older lots, and military bases, tourism, medical centers and higher education drive the present economy. Suburbs include Alamo Heights, Converse, Universal City, Terrell Hills and Castle Hills.

  • Typical monthly rent: $1,354

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page is the source for each of these.

Who values property in Bexar County, and who collects the tax?

Valuation and protests belong to the Bexar Central Appraisal District, and payments go to the Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector. BCAD's site says it takes no tax payments. It mails value notices to new owners and to anyone whose market value climbed $1,000 or more, and a protest can be filed without a notice.

The clerk's page gives 210-335-6628 for tax certificates and payment questions, at the Vista Verde Plaza Building. Across Texas, value is fixed each January 1, bills arrive in October, and unpaid tax turns delinquent February 1. School districts exempt $140,000 of a homestead, and seniors or disabled owners receive $60,000 on top.

Sellers should watch the lien. Texas attaches the year's tax lien to the land each January 1, which is why a closing agent wants a current tax certificate and proof that earlier years are paid.

It is $25.00 in all: $5.00 for recording, $10.00 for the records archive and $10.00 for records management. Extra pages are $4.00 each.

Which day of the month are Bexar County foreclosure auctions?

They happen on the first Tuesday of each month between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. If the first Tuesday is January 1 or July 4, the sale is held on the first Wednesday.

Can I order a certified copy of a Bexar County deed by mail?

Yes. Send the request to the clerk's office in the courthouse, or ask in person at the Deed Records Department in the Paul Elizondo Tower. The price is $1.00 a page and $5.00 for the certification.

Does the Bexar Central Appraisal District collect property tax?

No. BCAD handles values, exemptions and protests only. Tax payments and tax certificates go through the Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector at 210-335-6628.

Where do I record a deed in Tarrant County?

Land records go to the Records Intake office in Room B20 of the historic Tarrant County Courthouse, 100 W. Weatherford St., Fort Worth, TX 76196. The county says land-related documents can be recorded only there, not at the sub-courthouses.

You have three ways to file. Walk in during the posted hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday; mail the original with a check or money order payable to the Tarrant County Clerk; or use the county's eRecording process. In-person filers must show a driver's license or ID, while mailed documents do not need a copy of one.

The clerks cannot notarize a document, give legal advice or help fill in a form, so the deed must be notarized before you arrive. Intake also takes only originals or clerk-certified copies.

What does recording cost in Tarrant County?

How do I search Tarrant County property records?

Use the County Clerk Official Records Search, which is free to browse. Once you find a document you can register for an account and download an unofficial copy with a watermark at no charge, which is enough for your own research.

When a title company or lender needs a certified copy, the same system sells one online. You choose the certified-copy icon, pay the calculated fee, then pick the file up under Order History in your account. Certified copies are also sold in person at Room B30 of the courthouse or by mail with a self-addressed stamped envelope and the document number.

A new filing is not instant online. The county says recorded documents generally appear on the search site 5 to 7 business days after recording. Intake does the scanning and indexing while you wait and gives you an instrument number, so ask for that number if you need to prove the filing sooner. The county also says its staff do not run title searches, lien searches or restriction reviews, so that work stays with a title company.

What kinds of documents can the clerk record?

Intake accepts documents the law authorizes or permits to be recorded, mainly those tied to land. Deeds, deeds of trust, liens and lien releases, certain land-related affidavits and plats are the core examples.

The county turns away several categories:

  • Documents with no statutory authority behind their filing.
  • Documents that are not regular on their face.
  • Documents not properly signed in front of an officer such as a notary.
  • Copies that are neither originals nor clerk-certified.

Wills get special treatment. Intake records only probated wills, and a person who wants a will kept at the courthouse can leave it with the Probate office in Room B90 for a $5 fee. Texas law also requires a conveyance to be signed and acknowledged, or sworn before two witnesses, before it can be recorded. The state's county clerk manual lists the deed types seen most often: general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds.

Why do records matter when I sell a Tarrant County house?

A buyer's title company reads the recorded chain on your parcel before closing, and anything unreleased can delay the sale. Look for an old deed of trust with no release, a recorded lien, an affidavit that clouds title, or a missing deed from an inherited property.

Tax liens do not need a recording to exist. The state tax lien attaches on January 1 each year, and a buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid. State tax liens filed by the comptroller are recorded with the county clerk, so the clerk's records can show those too.

If a lender has started foreclosure, a notice of trustee sale appears in the clerk's records. Texas foreclosure sales are auctions, and for tax foreclosure the sale is run by a constable or an agent hired by the taxing unit. If you see a recorded notice against your house, you still have routes: pay off the debt, sell through a listing, or take a cash offer that closes before the sale date.

What else does the Tarrant County Clerk handle?

Under Texas practice the county clerk wears several hats: county recorder, clerk of the commissioners court, and the office that takes probate filings such as applications and small estate affidavits. In Tarrant County the real property side and the probate side sit in different rooms of the same courthouse, with probate in Room B90.

That split matters if you are selling a house that came to you through a death. The heirs may need probate papers on file before a deed can be signed, and those papers live in a different queue from the deed itself. Plan a trip, or a mailing, for each, and ask the title company which papers it needs recorded before closing.

Title companies and escrow agents also have account options. The county page lists an OPR Escrow Payments route for the Official Public Records, with 817-884-1062 for completing the process after an online payment, and a separate bulk data payment route with 817-884-1069. Most individual sellers will never need either, but your title company might use the first.

How can I watch for property fraud in Tarrant County?

Tarrant County offers a Property Fraud Alert sign-up, advertised on its Real Estate Records page. The county does not describe the details in the page text, so use the sign-up link there to see how alerts work and what they cover.

A practical habit is to search your own name and address on the Official Records Search once or twice a year. Look for deeds or liens you do not recognize. If you find one, bring the instrument number to the clerk's office and to a title company.

Recording is public by design. That helps buyers and lenders trust the chain of title, but it also means anyone can see what was filed against your parcel, and a forged deed that is recorded still has to be unwound through the courts.

Most documents cost $20 for the first page and $4 for each added page, per the county. A document printed on both sides counts as two pages.

Records Intake is in Room B20 of the Tarrant County Courthouse, 100 W. Weatherford St., Fort Worth, TX 76196. It is open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.

Can I record a deed by mail in Tarrant County?

Yes. Mail the original to Room B20 with a check or money order payable to the Tarrant County Clerk, and calculate the fee from the page count. The deed must already be notarized.

Can I get a copy of my deed for free?

Yes, an unofficial watermarked copy downloads free from the Official Records Search after you register for an account. Certified copies cost $1 per page plus $5 for certification.

How long before a recorded deed shows online in Tarrant County?

Generally 5 to 7 business days after recording. In-person filers get an instrument number and proof of recording while they wait.

Bring or mail the original signed document, because the clerk will not record a copy. Real property documents can be filed in person or by mail, and the clerk says recording is completed as soon as the document is received.

Who can file electronically in Travis County?

eRecording is limited to specific filers under Local Government Code Section 195.003, including licensed Texas attorneys, banks and credit unions, title insurance companies and agents, federally approved lenders, licensed regulated lenders and state agencies.

The clerk lists several approved submitter companies and invites anyone interested in becoming a submitter to contact the office. A homeowner selling alone does not qualify directly, so most sellers go through a title company, which typically e-files the deed on closing day.

What else should a Travis County seller know about the record?

Expect the record to show more than the deed: liens, trustee sale notices and tax liens are filed with the same clerk. Notice of a trustee sale of real estate is posted for a $2.00 fee, and state and federal tax liens have their own filing charges.

Property tax is a separate system: the appraisal district sets value and local taxing units bill, while the clerk only records documents. For closing figures, ask the Travis County tax office for the current bill. Before listing, search the owner's name for open liens and make sure the deed in your chain matches the name on the contract.

How do certified copies and older records work?

A certified copy is made by a clerk, who stamps it as an accurate and complete reproduction of the original. The clerk charges $5.00 per document for certification plus $1.00 per page, and certified copies can be requested by phone, email or in person.

The clerk's fee page adds that no recording sticker goes on the last page of a certified copy, so one extra $4.00 page is always added. Who records property documents in Hidalgo County?

Under the state constitution the clerk acts as "Recorder of the County," and the county's Recording page lists four tasks for each instrument: decide whether it will be accepted, file it, record it and index it.

Documents handled in the Recording Department include warranty deeds, trustee's deeds, tax liens, state and federal, foreclosures, judgments, subdivision plats and financing statements. The same department processes assumed name certificates, and since September 1, 2017 a county clerk may waive the fees for a military veteran who files one or files a statement of abandonment. A deed gets accepted only when the signer acknowledged it in front of a notary or comparable officer, or swore to it before two witnesses (Property Code 12.001(b)). File it in the county that contains the parcel.

Who values and taxes a Hidalgo County house?

The Hidalgo County Appraisal District, created on January 1, 1980, appraises property and administers exemptions for the county's taxing units. An eight-member board appointed by the taxing units governs it, and the county assessor-collector sits on the board as a voting member. Cities, school districts, utility districts and the county each set their own rate, and the district's values feed all of them.

Across Texas, value is fixed as of January 1, which is also the day the tax lien attaches. Bills go out around October 1 and turn delinquent on February 1, when a 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest are added. An owner who disagrees with a value can protest, and the usual cutoff is mid-May.

The district's public portal offers property valuations, tax information and online filing of appeals and exemptions. What record issues come up in Hidalgo County sales?

Four situations come up often: heirs, contract for deed sales, old liens and unpaid tax. Each leaves a trail at the clerk's office, and each is easier to fix before a buyer's title company finds it.

  • Unreleased deeds of trust. A paid loan with no recorded release still clouds title.

Sometimes. A transfer on death deed on record before the owner died, or a small estate affidavit for an estate of $75,000 or less (homestead and exempt property excluded), can move title without full administration. The buyer's title company decides whether to accept the paperwork.

Where is the Rockwall County Clerk's property records office?

The county's page warns that most GPS and internet maps place the building wrongly and says it sits about 0.3 miles east of Goliad and SH 205.

The Official Public Records can be searched online, and copies and eCertified copies can be bought there. Paper certified copies are mailed by the clerk's office. A buyer who picks "In Person" can fill a cart online but must pay at the counter.

One caution applies to the online search. A state law, House Bill 4350, took effect June 20, 2025 and requires information to be redacted from some instruments. Title examiners work from the official records, so a screen search is only a starting point.

What are the filing fees at the Rockwall County Clerk?

Expect $25 for page one and $4 for each page that follows. Senate Bill 1612 repealed the old $1 filing fee under Local Government Code Section 291.008(d) from January 1, 2024, and the county's fee list reflects that repeal.

What formatting rules does the Rockwall County Clerk enforce?

Paperwork gets turned away over format surprisingly often. The county's general requirements include:

  • Keep a 2-inch by 4-inch area empty at the foot of the final page, where the certification label is placed. If the area is crowded the label goes on the back, which adds a page and a $4 charge. E-filed documents follow the same rule.
  • Signatures must be originals or certified copies, since the clerk cannot file copies.
  • Print or type each name below its signature line.
  • An abstract of judgment that omits the plaintiff's address costs double to file.
  • A correction instrument has to conform to Texas Property Code Chapter 5.

Plats face a longer checklist. Sheet size runs from 18 by 24 inches up to 24 by 36, and the clerk wants a single black-line copy carrying the original seals and signatures, a full legal description, notarized signatures and a surveyor's certification. Inside a city's extraterritorial jurisdiction the city must approve it. Original tax certificates from every taxing unit, dated within 90 days of filing and showing no delinquent tax, must come with it.

What must a deed show before the clerk accepts it?

Under Property Code Section 12.001(b), the clerk can record a real property conveyance only when it carries a signature plus an acknowledgment or sworn statement before a notary or similar officer, or two subscribing witnesses. County clerks serve as recorders, and filing happens where the land is located.

Estate paperwork lands here too. For a muniment of title, the court order and will are lodged with the clerk in the property's county. A transfer on death deed has to be on record before the owner's death. The small estate affidavit suits an intestate estate worth $75,000 or less excluding the homestead, and a homestead copy is recorded with the clerk. An affidavit of heirship is only a sworn statement no court has checked, and nothing obliges a buyer or lender to rely on it.

A seller with a gap in the title should pull the chain of records early. A missing heir, an unreleased lien or an unrecorded deed will surface at the title company, and the cure usually means a fresh filing in this office.

Foreclosure notices are listed on the county's site. Trustee sales happen on the first Tuesday of each month outside on the courthouse steps at 1111 Yellowjacket Lane. State practice calls for the notice of sale to be filed with the clerk and posted at the courthouse door at least 21 days beforehand, and the auction takes place between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. After a notice of default, the borrower has 20 days to reinstate by paying what is past due.

Mechanic's liens have an exit in this office. Under Property Code Sections 53.171 to 53.174, anyone may file a bond to indemnify against a lien, and the lien is discharged once a compliant bond is filed, notice goes to each claimant by certified mail, and the bond and notice are recorded. The bond must generally be double the lien amount, or when the claims top $40,000, the larger of 1.5 times the liens or $40,000 plus the liens. The clerk charges the usual $25 and $4 page fees, plus $1 a page for copies and the mailing postage.

A free service called Property Fraud Alert sends a phone or email warning when a document is recorded under your name. One phone number can enroll 3 names and one email address can enroll 4.

The active units include Rockwall ISD and Royse City ISD, the cities of Rockwall, Fate, Royse City, Heath and McLendon-Chisholm, and parts of Wylie, Rowlett, Dallas and Garland. Seven municipal utility districts, three public improvement districts and the Club Municipal Management District #1 add more lines for some addresses.

Each year's tax lien takes hold on January 1 and the owner on that date answers for the bill. Liens for state taxes are entered by the clerk in the state tax lien book. For city permits or code questions, the county says to call the municipality if the property lies inside city limits. Outside city limits, its Development Services department covers the county engineer, GIS and 911 addressing, environmental health, fire marshal, and road and bridge.

On the first Tuesday of every month, at the front steps of the Rockwall County Courthouse. Direct questions to the trustee named on a notice, and see the county's foreclosure notices page for the listings.

What is Brazoria County like, and how does the land affect records?

Brazoria County is a 1,407 square mile Gulf Coast county at the mouth of the Brazos River, and flood and hurricane exposure shapes how its land is held and insured. The Handbook of Texas notes 52 inches of annual rainfall, a long list of historic hurricanes and floods, and soils that are productive when well drained.

The county was created in 1836, and Angleton replaced the town of Brazoria as seat in 1896. Pearland is the largest city, and Brazosport is a community of nine cities that includes Lake Jackson, Clute, Freeport and Surfside Beach. State highways 6, 35, 36 and 288 serve the area. The economy leans on petrochemicals, with Dow Chemical arriving at Freeport in 1939, plus agriculture, fishing and tourism.

The district also describes a homestead audit program under Senate Bill 1801, which requires each residence homestead exemption to be reviewed at least once every five tax years. Owners who get no letter need not file again. The Tax Assessor-Collector's office, at 111 E. Locust in Angleton, is listed at 979-864-1320 for tax bills.

On the state side, the school district homestead exemption is $140,000, and owners 65 or older or disabled receive $60,000 more. A tax lien attaches every January 1, and delinquent taxes after January 31 carry penalty and interest. What recording problems slow a Brazoria County sale?

The usual culprits are missing notary details, a legal description that does not match the prior deed, and unreleased liens. A release of a paid-off lien is itself a recordable instrument, so ask the lender for it in writing and confirm it appears in the clerk's index.

Inherited houses need extra proof. The State Law Library says an affidavit of heirship is a sworn, court-unverified statement filed with the county clerk, and no law forces third parties to accept it. An order from the probate court, or a transfer on death deed recorded before the owner's death, gives a buyer firmer footing.

Foreclosure timing also shows up in these records. A notice of sale must be posted at the courthouse and filed with the clerk at least 21 days before the first-Tuesday auction, and Brazoria County charges $8.00 for a trustee notice.

No. The clerks are recorders and are not qualified examiners, so you search the online database yourself or use the public computers at 237 East Locust in Angleton.

The clerk adds a penalty fee. Texas Property Code 11.003 sets it at the greater of $25 or twice the statutory filing fee, charged on top of the regular recording cost.

You can view and buy copies through the clerk's online Self-Service portal or on the computers in the office lobby, and archived record books can be read in the office. The clerk's office has three divisions: Records, Courts and Commissioners Court. Probate and guardianship support sits with the Courts Division, which matters when the owner of a house has died.   • Each deed of trust, then a matching release. A loan paid off years ago can still show as open if the release was never filed.
  • Judgments, abstracts and state tax liens. The state clerk manual says the Comptroller files state tax lien notices with the county clerk, who records them in a state tax lien book.

The state clerk manual names the usual instruments in the deed records: general and special warranty deeds, quitclaim deeds, trustee's deeds, sheriff's deeds, tax deeds, affidavits, releases of deeds of trust, leases, contracts of sale and powers of attorney. A missing grantee mailing address can add $25. Get the current total from the Hays clerk before you mail anything.

An owner who gets an audit letter should answer it with a copy of a valid Texas driver's license or state ID whose address matches the house. Old liens, unpaid tax and missing heirs top the list. Each January 1 a Texas tax lien attaches to secure that year's bill, so an unpaid balance travels with the house through a sale. Tax still open after January 31 turns delinquent on February 1 with a 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest.

The clerk's FAQ gives the reason for the service: scammers record fake deeds to pose as owners, then collect rent or sale money from victims. When does the Leon County Clerk stop taking documents, and what does recording cost?

The office runs 7:45 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. each weekday without a lunch closure, yet recording itself ends at 4 p.m. Whatever arrives after that goes onto the next business day's work. The office takes cash, checks and major credit cards.

The posted charge is $15 for page one of an instrument and $4 for each page after it, under a schedule the office says began on January 1, 2024. Electronic filing into the official records runs through three named vendors, Simplifile, CSC and ePN. Fees shift over time, so verify the amount with the clerk's staff first.

Different deputies take different work. General recording, indexing and copy requests sit with the chief deputy, while probate, civil filings, marriage licenses and vital records each have their own staff member and phone menu option, so say at the start of a call that you are asking about recording a deed. What does Texas require before a Leon County deed can be recorded?

A land conveyance may be recorded only after the owner signs it and swears to it or acknowledges it, either before two witnesses or before an officer such as a notary, county clerk, district clerk or county court judge (Property Code 12.001(b)).

The 2023 county clerk manual describes the instruments that land in deed records: general and special warranty deeds, quitclaims, trustee's deeds, sheriff's deeds and tax deeds, plus lien releases, affidavits and contracts of sale. Nobody can go back and write new heirs into an old deed. After an owner's death, the manual points to an executor's or administrator's deed for an administered estate, a court order with the will for a muniment of title, or an affidavit of heirship when nothing else is available.

Leon County is rural, east of Waco on Interstate 45 between Dallas and Houston. Census estimates for July 2025 count 16,894 people, up 7.2 percent since 2020. Within 1,073.16 square miles of land are 9,255 housing units and 6,741 households.

According to the Handbook of Texas, the county was carved from Robertson County in 1846. Leona served first as seat of government, and Centerville took over in 1851. Buffalo is the biggest community, and Jewett, Normangee, Oakwood and Marquez are also named. U.S. 79 crosses east to west, the Trinity River marks the eastern edge, and Lake Limestone fills part of the northwest corner. Oil and gas, agribusiness and lumber anchor the economy.

The Leon Central Appraisal District sets values and the county tax assessor-collector issues bills. The county's page directs owners with account changes or value questions to the appraisal district at 141 W. St. Mary's, Centerville, TX 75833, telephone 903-536-2252.

If a collection letter shows up, the unit that sent it tells you which firm to contact.

Statewide, values freeze as of January 1, bills show up in October, and penalty-free payment ends January 31. A tax lien takes hold every January 1, so a Leon County house enters any sale still owing that year's tax. Our Leon County property tax guide covers the tax office itself.

  • Heirs can file a sworn heirship statement with the Leon County Clerk, though nothing obliges a buyer or lender to rely on it.

Where are Washington County property records kept?

Real property documents go to the Washington County Clerk, 100 East Main Street, Suite 102, in Brenham. The county's own welcome page calls Washington County "the Birth Place of Texas."

The clerk doubles as county recorder, and land instruments go to the clerk serving the parcel. A deed for a house in Chappell Hill, Burton, Independence or Gay Hill goes to the same Brenham office as a deed for a house in Brenham itself. Those community names appear in the Texas State Library's list of the county's old justice precinct records, which is a handy reminder of how the county is divided.

How do I search Washington County deed records online?

The clerk's recording page says Official Public Records are available online through eDocTec, and that deed records and official public records are online from 1836 to the present. Use the index to find an instrument, then ask the clerk about copies.

Records from before the modern index exist in other forms too. The Texas State Library lists the county's deed record for 1834 to 1904 on microfilm held at Texas A&M University in College Station, with direct and reverse indexes on separate reels. The same list covers probate minutes, probate records, marriage records from 1837 and tax rolls from 1837 to 1910. An old family farm may need that older chain of title when a buyer's title company starts its search.

  • Begin with the current owner's name and latest deed, then trace each deed of trust and release.
  • Look for liens, easements and affidavits recorded after the deed.
  • For a plat, ask the clerk for a copy; the county lists $10.00 for a plat copy.

Ask the clerk for the exact total on your document before you mail it, because the clerk's page and the manual do not break the fees down the same way.

Mail documents to the Washington County Clerk, 100 East Main Street, Suite 102, Brenham, TX 77833, with the correct filing fee. The county also notes that a plat needs a current tax certificate showing no delinquent ad valorem taxes.

What does a deed need before the Brenham clerk will record it?

A deed must be an original, properly notarized or certified by the recording office of another county, state or country. The clerk's page adds that documents must meet any requirements set out in Texas statute.

The state clerk manual cites Property Code 12.001(b): a land conveyance is recordable only when signed and acknowledged, either before an authorized officer such as a notary or before two subscribing witnesses. Its list of recordable items includes warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds, plus releases, leases, contracts of sale and powers of attorney. A missing grantee mailing address can add a $25 charge.

  • Use the original signed document, not a photocopy.
  • Get the signature acknowledged by a notary or another authorized officer.
  • Include the grantee's mailing address.
  • Send the fee for the first page, added pages and any extra names.

Commissioners courts may waive land recording fees for buyers in certain grant programs, so ask the clerk whether that applies to yours.

How do inheritance and probate filings show up in Washington County records?

They appear as recorded instruments that connect the owner on the old deed to the heirs. Which instrument you need depends on whether the estate went through court.

The State Law Library lists the routes. Four tools matter at the recording counter. A transfer on death deed avoids probate when it is recorded ahead of the owner's death. A muniment of title uses the court order and the will. A small estate affidavit fits estates of $75,000 or less, apart from the homestead, and needs court approval. An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement that a title company may refuse.

  • Administered estate: an executor's or administrator's deed.
  • Will without administration: a court order and the will.
  • Transfer on death deed: record an affidavit of death with the death certificate.
  • No court action: an affidavit of heirship, which a buyer may question.

Heirs are never added to the old deed. A new instrument is recorded.

How do foreclosure and tax liens appear in Washington County records?

Sale notices for foreclosures go on the courthouse door and into the clerk's files at least 21 days ahead, and the clerk's page lists the postings.

Sales are public auctions, held in a county-designated area between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on a month's first Tuesday. A borrower generally has 20 days from the default notice to reinstate. State tax liens are different. The Comptroller files notice with the county clerk, who records it in the state tax lien book, and a federal tax lien recorded with the clerk draws the $30.00 fee shown above.

Ordinary property tax liens begin each January 1 and do not show up as recorded deeds. Ask the county tax office for a tax certificate before closing; plats also need one.

What should a Washington County seller check before closing?

Pull the deed and every recorded lien for the address, and confirm that every release has been filed. A title company will do the same, but finding a gap early saves time.

  • Search the online index for the current deed, deeds of trust, releases and affidavits.
  • Confirm that the owner on the deed matches the person selling, or record the heirship instrument first.
  • Ask the county for a tax certificate and pay delinquent taxes from proceeds if needed.
  • Look for a posted foreclosure notice if a payment has been missed.
  • Check a plat if the lot was recently divided.

Whatever is recorded against the property will surface in the buyer's title search.

The county lists $70.00 per slide to file a plat and $10.00 for a copy. A plat needs a tax certificate showing no delinquent ad valorem taxes, among other items.

Does Washington County record transfer on death deeds?

The clerk records deeds for the county, and state guidance says a transfer on death deed has to be recorded before the owner dies. File it with the clerk where the land sits.

Who do I call at the clerk's office?

The clerk's page lists 979-277-6216 for marriage license appointments, and that is the number to try for questions about the office. Ask about hours and recording in the same call.

Where do I search and record property records in Bell County?

Deeds, liens and plats for Bell County are filed with the County Clerk in Belton, and the Property Records/Recordings desk answers at (254) 933-5171. The clerk works from the Bell County Justice Center at 1201 Huey Road, Belton, TX 76513, weekdays from 8 in the morning to 5 in the afternoon, and takes mail at P.O. Box 480 in Belton.

Electronic filing is limited to the entities named in Local Government Code 195.003, such as attorneys, banks and title companies. How is Bell County laid out, and what does that mean for a records search?

Bell County is a 1,055 square mile county in east central Texas, roughly 45 miles north of Austin, and its records cover very different kinds of land. The Handbook of Texas describes the Balcones Escarpment running through the middle, with level Blackland Prairie farmland to the east and rolling Grand Prairie uplands to the west.

The county was formed in 1850 and its seat, first called Nolanville, took the name Belton in 1851. Today Killeen is the largest city, and Temple grew up around the Santa Fe railroad headquarters in 1881. Other towns include Harker Heights, Nolanville, Salado and Morgan's Point Resort. Interstate 35 and U.S. 190 are the main roads, and Belton Lake and Stillhouse Hollow Lake shape the lakeside lots.

That mix produces the paperwork variety a title searcher sees here: old farm tracts with metes and bounds descriptions, subdivision plats around Killeen and Temple, lakefront parcels, and homes near Fort Cavazos, the military post in the western part of the county.

  • Typical monthly rent: $1,224
  • Veterans in the county: 48,220

The Bell Central Appraisal District sets value, and the clerk only records the deed. The district keeps three public offices: Belton at 411 E. Central (254-939-5841), Killeen at 301 Priest Dr. (254-634-9752) and Temple at 205 E. Central (254-771-1108). All three open weekdays until 4:45 p.m., and one mailing box, P.O. Box 390 in Belton, serves them.

Its contact page sends deed and address-change questions to a mapping email, which matters after a sale: a recorded deed is what lets the district update ownership. Protests have their own address, and the district says protests will not be accepted at any other inbox.

Appraisals reflect ownership and condition on each January 1, with homestead notices mailed around April 1. A protest is due May 15 or 30 days from delivery of the notice, whichever falls later. Schools exempt $140,000 of a homestead's value, and owners aged 65 and up or with a disability get another $60,000.

Whatever is recorded against the house shows up in the title search and can delay closing until it is paid or released. The Comptroller explains that each year's tax lien attaches January 1, and whoever owned the house on that day stays liable for that bill even after selling.

Foreclosure is visible in the same records. Trustees post a sale notice at the courthouse and file a copy with the clerk 21 or more days ahead, and the auction runs the first Tuesday of the month from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Bell County's schedule lists foreclosure postings at $2.00 when the trustee does it and $12.00 when the clerk posts.

Inherited houses add another layer. The State Law Library describes an affidavit of heirship as a sworn statement placed on file with the clerk, and nothing obliges a buyer or lender to rely on it. A deed that transfers property at death has to be recorded while the owner is alive, and a muniment of title order and will go to the clerk where the land lies.

Daily business transactions end at 4:30 p.m., and 4:15 p.m. applies on the last business day of the month, so month-end closings need documents delivered ahead of time.

Where do I find McLennan County property records?

The McLennan County Clerk keeps the county's deed records in Waco, on the second floor of the Records Building at 215 N 5th Street, Room 223. Call 254-757-5078 to reach the counter, which opens on weekdays from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m. and closes on county holidays.

The same office also holds liens, hospital liens, cattle brands, assumed name certificates and marriage licenses, and it clerks the probate court and the commissioners' court. For a seller, one counter therefore holds most of what a title company asks for. Staff will not interpret a document, so legal questions go to an attorney or a legal aid group.

In Texas the county clerk doubles as county recorder, and a deed is filed where the land lies. A house anywhere in McLennan County is recorded in this office, wherever its owner lives.

How far back do the McLennan County records go?

Clerk records begin in 1849 and continue to the present, divided between bound volumes and an electronic system. Anything recorded on or after January 1, 1996 can be searched online or on public workstations in the clerk's office, the county says.

The middle rows overlap because the county lists its older material in more than one place. For a deed recorded before 1996, phone the clerk first and ask which format holds it.

How do I search the McLennan County records?

Search by name. McLennan County does not index by legal description, the clerk says, so you need the grantor or the grantee, which means the seller or the buyer named on the deed.

  • The Online Records Search, linked from the clerk's Official Public Records page, covers everything recorded since 1996.
  • The public workstations in the Records Building cover older volumes and anything the online tool leaves out.
  • A survey is unlikely to turn up. Surveys are not recordable by themselves in Texas, so the county has one only when it rode along as an exhibit to another document, which seldom happens.

Note the volume and page or the instrument number of each document you locate, so the title company can order exact copies instead of searching again.

What does McLennan County require to record a deed?

The clerk posts a short list of filing standards, and a document that misses one comes back unrecorded. The office adds that it will record only finished documents that meet those standards and cannot advise on legal matters.

  • The land must lie in McLennan County, and any real property document needs a legal description.
  • Signatures must be originals, proved, acknowledged or sworn to as Texas law requires.
  • Only originals are accepted, apart from certified copies issued by another government agency.
  • It needs a heading naming its type, must be written in English, and must show a return address.
  • A deed also needs the grantee's address, which the clerk says serves tax purposes.
  • Payment options: cash, cashier's or business checks, money orders, personal checks, and Visa, MasterCard or American Express.

Two practical points come from the clerk's FAQ. Nobody at the counter can notarize your signature, so get the deed acknowledged beforehand, and the recorded original goes back by mail the next business day.

The Texas Courts county clerk manual describes the statutory base: $5.00 for page one, $4.00 for each additional page, and $0.25 per name beyond five that has to be indexed. Add-on fees include up to $10 for records management, up to $10 for a records archive and $2.00 for technology.

Leaving the grantee's mailing address off a deed can add $25. The county posts its own Recording Fee Schedule as a PDF on the Official Public Records page, so rely on that for the exact total and confirm it with the clerk or title company before you write a check.

What if the records show a lien, an old foreclosure or an unknown heir?

The title company searches these records ahead of closing, which is when loose ends appear. Typical finds include a mortgage paid off with no release on file, a hospital lien, a mechanic's lien, or a deed signed by a relative who has died.

  • Unpaid property tax stays with the house. The county's tax office calls taxes delinquent if unpaid before February 1 of the next year, and its tax sales run online through GovEase.
  • The trustee named on each notice conducts a foreclosure sale, and the clerk does not. Sales are held on the outside steps at the 2nd floor entrance of the courthouse at 501 Washington Ave., usually starting at 10:00 a.m., and the notices can be read at the clerk's office.
  • An inherited house can be sorted out through probate, and the County Clerk keeps those case files. An affidavit of heirship can also be recorded with the clerk, though the State Law Library points out that no law makes anyone accept it.

When a record problem is holding up a sale, a buyer who purchases as-is and works through the title company may handle the cleanup as part of closing.

Who appraises McLennan County property, and when is a protest due?

Values for county tax purposes come from the McLennan Central Appraisal District at 315 S 26th Street, Waco. A spring Notice of Appraised Value goes to owners whose market value rose by at least $1,000, and the district puts the protest deadline at May 15 or 30 days after mailing, whichever falls later.

A filed protest first gets an informal meeting with an appraiser, and an unsettled case moves to the Appraisal Review Board. Online protests for most residential property run April 10 through May 15, per the district. Homestead exemptions use Form 50-114 and are generally due by April 30.

The deed index does not show the tax bill, so a buyer should ask the McLennan County Tax Office for the account status. A tax lien attaches each January 1, and the owner that day answers for that year.

How large is McLennan County?

The Census Bureau put McLennan County at 272,020 people as of July 1, 2025, compared with 260,579 in the 2020 census and 234,906 in 2010. The county has 1,036.66 square miles of land and held 251.4 people a mile in 2020.

For 2020 through 2024, 61.8% of homes were lived in by their owners, and the midpoint home value was $243,600. Gross rent at the midpoint was $1,173 and household income at the midpoint was $66,643, across 97,338 households of about 2.64 people. The Bureau also lists 1,442 building permits for 2025 and 112,290 housing units in mid-2025.

Have the title company compare the recorded deed, the tax account and the seller's name early, so a mismatch surfaces well before closing.

Is there a way to find a McLennan County deed from a street address?

No. Records are indexed by name, not legal description, so you need the grantor or grantee. Online Records Search handles 1996 onward, and the Records Building workstations handle older volumes.

Where is the McLennan County Clerk's office?

Room 223 of the McLennan County Records Building, 215 N 5th Street, Waco, TX 76701, telephone 254-757-5078, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. except holidays.

Can the clerk's office notarize my deed?

No notary works at the counter, per the clerk's FAQ. Sign in front of a notary elsewhere and bring the original, because copies are not accepted.

Does the County Clerk run the foreclosure sale?

No, the trustee named on each notice runs it. Sales happen on the courthouse steps at 501 Washington Ave., Waco, and notices are available at the clerk's office.

How do I find out whether back taxes are owed on a McLennan County house?

Ask the McLennan County Tax Office, which treats a bill as delinquent when unpaid before February 1 of the next year. The title company's commitment will show unpaid tax as well.

Where do I find and record property records in King County, Texas?

Three offices in Guthrie split the work on any parcel. The clerk keeps recorded documents, the chief appraiser keeps value and exemption files, and the tax assessor-collector sends statements and takes payments. Each lists its own post office box on the county website.

Texas will not let a clerk record a land conveyance unless the signature was acknowledged, or sworn before two witnesses (Property Code 12.001(b)). That manual also explains how the bill is built. Page one carries $5.00 and each added page $4.00 under Local Government Code 118.012, and records management, archive and technology charges come on top within statutory caps. Because each county picks its own add-ons, the King County total will differ from the base numbers, so ask the office for the whole amount.

Land records follow the land. A deed for a King County house goes to Guthrie, wherever the seller now lives, whether that is Lubbock, Wichita Falls or another state.

King County is among the smallest counties in the nation by population. Census Bureau figures show about 192 people for mid-2025, against 265 in the 2020 count and 286 in 2010. Its 910.87 square miles of land hold roughly 0.3 people per square mile.

The Handbook of Texas places the county in the Rolling Prairie region of northwest Texas, with Cottle, Foard, Knox, Stonewall and Dickens counties around it. The legislature created it on August 21, 1876, and it was organized in 1891 with Guthrie as county seat. Big ranches drove its early story: the Four Sixes, the Pitchfork, the Matador and the SMS. Oil came in 1943, and beef cattle remain the main farm product. U.S. 83 runs north and south, U.S. 82 east and west, and Dumont and Finney are the other named communities.   • Old mortgage. A paid-off lender should sign a release, which the clerk records like any other instrument. Request one if the payoff happened years ago.
